questions.q: In which decade did archaeologists begin the discovery of the major sites of the Harappan Civilisation?
questions.a: The discovery began in the 1920s. A wrong answer here suggests the student has not distinguished between the historical period of the civilisation (2600 BCE) and the time it was "discovered" by modern historians.

questions.q: Why do historians classify the Harappan Civilisation as an "urban" civilisation?
questions.a: It is called urban because it featured large, complex cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro rather than small, scattered farming hamlets. A wrong answer indicates the student does not understand the difference between a simple village and a planned, city-based society.

questions.q: If an archaeologist finds a Harappan site, does it automatically belong to the 2600 BCE–1900 BCE period? Explain your reasoning.
questions.a: Not necessarily; they must use carbon dating or compare the pottery/artifacts found to known Harappan styles to confirm the date. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks all ancient ruins are from the same time period.

questions.q: How does the vast geographical extent (1.2 million square kilometres) change our understanding of these early people?
questions.a: It shows they were not an isolated group but a vast network of connected cities across a huge region. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks of the civilisation as a small, single town rather than a widespread culture.

questions.q: Could we call the Harappan Civilisation "modern" because it had cities? Justify your stance.
questions.a: No, we call it "early urban," because while they had cities, they lacked modern technology like electricity or the internet. The student must distinguish between the structure of a society (cities) and the level of technology.

questions.q: Imagine you are an archaeologist. What clues would you look for to prove a newly discovered site is part of the Harappan Civilisation?
questions.a: I would look for specific styles of baked bricks, urban planning (grid patterns), and types of pottery or seals characteristic of the Harappan culture. A poor answer would focus on vague items like "old tools" which could belong to any time period.
